title: To Debate in 2028, Democrats Will Have to Disavow Dark Money
author: Rebecca Schneid
body:
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) on Monday announced plans for 12 debates in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, beginning in June 2027. The framework, released earlier than usual, includes a new requirement: To qualify for the debates, candidates must sign a pledge to denounce certain outside spending.

Candidates will need to sign the newly released Fair Campaign Practices Pledge, denouncing both super PAC spending and “dark money,” which is any political funding from undisclosed sources. Otherwise, they will be ineligible to take part in the party’s official debates, which are a critical way for candidates to gain support and share their priorities with voters.

“The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House,” DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement Monday.

But the requirement raises questions about enforcement and effectiveness, experts tell TIME.

Read more: Inside the Democrats' Plans to Take On Trump

The announcement follows historic 2026 midterm wins for Democrats, who will now hold 258 seats in the House of Representatives and a majority in the Senate—the party’s biggest sweep since the early 1990s. The election cycle set new spending records: According to AdImpact, political advertisers spent $12.06 billion leading up to the 2026 midterms, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle.

While the biggest donors in this year’s election disproportionately favored Republicans, Daniel Weiner, a campaign finance expert at Brennan Center for Justice, sees the DNC’s announcement as a move to address the American public’s general concerns about corruption in politics.

A Brennan Center analysis published Oct. 28 found that 92% of registered voters surveyed nationwide saw corruption in politics and government as a very or moderately big problem.

“I think the role of dark money in our elections feeds into voters' sense that their government isn't working for them,” Weiner says. In the same survey, 88% of voters blamed corruption for the government’s failure to solve major problems such as the economy.

It also potentially signals that other meaningful changes are in store when Democrats take control of Congress in January, he adds.

On its own, however, Weiner says that the pledge stipulation is “not itself a huge accomplishment.” In order to reinforce the party’s anti-corruption position, Democratic lawmakers will need to introduce legislation that curbs outside spending, he says.

“It's great that they want to clean up their primary, but the question is: What will they do to actually wield power?” Weiner says.

How will the DNC enforce its 2028 primary debate rules?

Under the DNC’s new rules for the Democratic primary, candidates will need to sign the Fair Campaign Practices Pledge, disavowing spending by super PACs, which can raise unlimited amounts of money from individuals and corporations, and dark money organizations—which are 501(c)(4) nonprofit groups that do not have to disclose donor lists.

Each campaign that signs the pledge will designate a representative who can report outside spending to the DNC. The DNC will review complaints and notify campaigns if a candidate must denounce the spending. A candidate who misses the deadline will be disqualified from that debate and any subsequent debates until they denounce it. The DNC says it will publish a tracker showing complaints, their status, and candidates’ denunciations.

Candidates need to denounce each group’s spending only once, and the groups can keep running the ads. How the DNC will apply the rule in practice, and whether it will deter outside spending, remains to be seen.

“It's too soon to tell,” Weiner says of potential enforcement opportunities. “I think it's going to be enforceable certainly in extreme cases, if a candidate is quite obviously collaborating with a dark money group, then it seems pretty clear they shouldn't be eligible to participate in the debate.”

Robert Boatright, a political science professor at Clark University, says that calling on candidates to “denounce” these groups is “slippery.”

“Probably the biggest loophole here is if you have a super PAC that is not supporting anybody in particular, but is really opposed to a particular candidate, then they could campaign against that candidate,” he tells TIME.

Candidates may benefit from those opposition ads but can also distance themselves from the groups behind the messaging. Worth noting, however, is that if a covered ad attacks one candidate, the DNC requires every opponent to denounce the spending.

The move can also potentially be enforced through the court of public opinion, Boatwright suggests. If a candidate is caught colluding with super PACs or dark money groups—especially if they have pledged not to—then it could significantly ding their trustworthiness and harm their campaign, he explains.

“I think the norms in the Democratic Party are such that a candidate would take a big hit in public opinion from violating this,” he says.

What is ‘dark money’ in elections?

Dark money refers to election spending whose original funding sources are hidden from the public. While super PACs must disclose donors, those donors can include organizations that do not identify their own funders.

These nonprofit, tax-exempt groups—such as 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations and 501(c)(6) trade associations—are allowed to engage in political activity as long as it is not their primary purpose.

Read more: How Profits Took Over American Politics

According to government transparency nonprofit OpenSecrets, dark money groups have spent roughly $1 billion—mainly on television commercials, online ads, and print mailers—to influence elections since Citizens United v. FEC Supreme Court. That 2010 Supreme Court ruling revolutionized campaign finance law, striking down restrictions on independent election spending by corporations and unions.

A federal appeals court ruling later that year, SpeechNow.org v. FEC, helped pave the way for super PACs by ending limits on contributions to groups that make only independent expenditures.

Super PACs subsequently became a fixture of the political landscape and have steadily gained influence. But that influence is not evenly distributed.

David Meyers, a spokesperson for OpenSecrets, estimates that dark-money spending in the 2020 Democratic presidential primary totaled about $5 million, which he calls a “drop in the bucket.” Issue One, a campaign finance watchdog, puts total outside spending in that primary at about $52 million.

It's notable that the DNC’s rules only apply to the primaries—not the general election, Meyers says.

While he doesn’t believe that the pledge requirement will keep dark money out of politics, even for Democrats, Meyers does hope it will limit party infighting ahead of the consequential presidential election.

“If the Democrats hold to this, and the candidates really do denounce any outside spending, we may be less likely to see attack ads from super PACs,” Meyers says, explaining that such tactics require the targets of those ads to expend valuable resources defending themselves, whether the claims in the ads had any basis in reality or not.

He points to super PAC-funded attack ads during the 2020 Democratic primary between Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg of Indiana.

Outside ad attacks can also prompt retaliation, which he believes is not a good use of Democrats’ time, money, or focus as the party works to take back the White House.

“I think this is really more about protecting the party's candidates,” Meyers says.
